title: Choosing a Partner: Layers, Self-Avoidance and Smell

generated.pipeline: extract → Codex draft → Codex accuracy gate + fix (fresh context)

cards.front: A neuron's whole branched tree is its {{c1::arbor}}.
cards.quote: Its arbor is its whole branched tree.

cards.front: Why are molecular labels useful after a gradient has guided an axon to a target region?
cards.back: Gradients establish continuous positional order. Labels help make discrete choices, such as which layer to occupy or which cells count as self.
cards.quote: A gradient is good at continuous order: neighbouring points in the eye map to neighbouring points in the tectum.
cards.section: Labels, not gradients

cards.front: Why can binding between identical surface proteins bring some neuronal processes together but drive others apart?
cards.back: Binding identifies a match; the cellular response determines adhesion or retreat. Shared group labels can gather processes, while individual identities can separate sister branches.
cards.quote: A match between identical surface proteins only tells two membranes "we are the same". The cell decides what "same" means.
cards.section: Labels, not gradients

cards.front: Two neuronal processes carry matching surface labels, and recognition is intact. Is this enough to predict whether they will stick together on contact, and why?
cards.back: No. The match supplies recognition; the cellular response determines whether they stick together or pull apart.
cards.quote: If each cell carries its own combination and the response is to retreat, that cell's own branches spread apart while it still overlaps its neighbours.
cards.section: Labels, not gradients

cards.front: Which three retinal cell classes make synapses in the inner plexiform layer?
cards.back: Bipolar cells, amacrine cells and retinal ganglion cells.
cards.quote: The inner plexiform layer of the retina is a thin band where bipolar cells, amacrine cells and retinal ganglion cells make synapses.
cards.section: Same means stick: layers in the retina

cards.front: Binding of a cell-surface protein to its own kind is called {{c1::homophilic binding}}.
cards.quote: Each binds its own kind, which is called homophilic binding.
cards.section: Same means stick: layers in the retina

cards.front: How can a retinal process reach the correct broad region yet encounter the wrong synaptic partners?
cards.back: It can arborise in the wrong sublamina. Different cell types send processes into particular sublaminae, so sublaminar position changes which partners they meet.
cards.quote: It is divided into thinner sublaminae, and each cell type sends its processes into one or a few of them.
cards.section: Same means stick: layers in the retina

cards.front: Which four homophilic proteins form the described chick retinal sublaminar label set?
cards.back: Sidekick-1, Sidekick-2, Dscam and DscamL.
cards.quote: In 2008 Yamagata and Sanes extended the set to four proteins, adding Dscam and DscamL, each marking a different group of cells and sublaminae.
cards.section: Same means stick: layers in the retina

cards.front: Chick retinal cells gain a Sidekick protein they normally lack, and their arbors shift toward the sublamina already rich in it. How does this distinguish a targeting cue from a passive marker?
cards.back: The shift supports an instructive contribution: changing the label changes arbor location. It does not show that Sidekick alone assigns every layer.
cards.quote: They shifted toward the sublamina where that Sidekick was already concentrated: adding the label moved the arbor.
cards.section: Same means stick: layers in the retina

cards.front: What observation supports calling a developmental signal instructive rather than merely correlated with an outcome?
cards.back: Changing where the signal is present makes the outcome follow it. The signal therefore helps direct the outcome.
cards.quote: This is a test worth recognising: move the signal, and see whether the outcome follows.
cards.section: Same means stick: layers in the retina

cards.front: A mouse retinal neuron lacking DSCAM has bundled dendrites. Must its arbor also occupy the wrong sublamina, and why?
cards.back: No. Mouse cells lacking DSCAM or DSCAML1 can still reach the right sublaminae. A spacing defect does not imply a sublaminar targeting defect.
cards.quote: mouse cells lacking DSCAM or DSCAML1 still reach the right sublaminae, so mouse sublaminae are not simply assigned by these four proteins.
cards.section: Same means stick: layers in the retina

cards.front: Recognition and separation of a neuron's own sister branches is called {{c1::self-avoidance}}.
cards.quote: It requires each branch to recognise sister branches from the same cell and move away from them.
cards.section: A badge only you wear: self-avoidance

cards.front: What pattern of surface identities allows sister branches to avoid each other while neighbouring neurons can overlap?
cards.back: Sister branches carry matching identities; neighbouring neurons carry distinguishable identities. Matching triggers retreat within a neuron without routinely excluding its neighbours.
cards.quote: Every branch of one neuron must carry the same version, so that sister branches always match.
cards.section: A badge only you wear: self-avoidance

cards.front: Different forms of one protein made from a single gene are called {{c1::isoforms}}.
cards.quote: Forms of one protein made from a single gene are called isoforms.
cards.section: A badge only you wear: self-avoidance

cards.front: How does one fly Dscam1 gene generate many protein isoforms?
cards.back: Alternative splicing keeps one exon from each of four alternative-exon clusters in each messenger RNA, generating different combinations.
cards.quote: Each messenger RNA keeps exactly one exon from each cluster, a choice called alternative splicing:
cards.section: A badge only you wear: self-avoidance

cards.front: Fly Dscam1 chooses one exon from each cluster of 12, 48 and 33 outer-domain alternatives, plus one of 2 membrane-spanning alternatives. How many distinct outer domains and total isoforms can it make?
cards.back: Outer domains: 12 × 48 × 33 = 19,008. Total isoforms: 19,008 × 2 = 38,016. The membrane-spanning choice doubles total isoforms without changing the outer surface.
cards.quote: The fourth cluster builds the stretch that crosses the membrane, so it does not change the outer surface.
cards.section: A badge only you wear: self-avoidance

cards.front: Remove Dscam1 from just one fly sensory neuron, leaving neighbouring neurons unchanged. What happens to contacts between its own dendritic branches, and why?
cards.back: Its own branches cross and bundle. Loss of Dscam1 removes the recognition-dependent repulsion that normally separates sister branches.
cards.quote: Binding is homophilic, as with Sidekick, but here the outcome is repulsion: when two branches carrying the same isoforms touch, they pull apart.
cards.section: A badge only you wear: self-avoidance

cards.front: Giving one Dscam1-deficient fly neuron a single isoform restores separation of its own branches while its neighbours remain normal. What does this show about isoform diversity?
cards.back: One isoform can supply self-recognition within a neuron. A large repertoire is needed to distinguish different neurons, rather than to separate one cell's sister branches.
cards.quote: The third row shows that one isoform is enough for self-recognition: what matters is that every branch of one cell carries the same one.
cards.section: A badge only you wear: self-avoidance

cards.front: A fly population retains Dscam1 binding but every neuron now displays the same single ectodomain isoform. What interaction is predicted between normally overlapping neighbours, and why?
cards.back: They are predicted to avoid each other because neighbours now match as sister branches do. Severe circuit disorganisation was observed; the avoidance outcome follows the recognition rule.
cards.quote: Neighbours that carry the same single isoform cannot tell themselves from each other, so their branches meet as if they were sister branches,
cards.section: A badge only you wear: self-avoidance

cards.front: Why does a distinctive Dscam1 identity not require every neuron to have completely non-overlapping isoforms?
cards.back: Identity depends on distinguishable combinations. Sister branches match across their sets, while neighbours may share some isoforms and still differ; the retreat threshold is not established.
cards.quote: So "unique" means a distinguishable combination, not zero overlap: sister branches carry matching sets, while a neighbour can share some isoforms and still differ.
cards.section: A badge only you wear: self-avoidance

cards.front: Why should mouse retinal DSCAM not be treated as a fly-like per-neuron identity code?
cards.back: Vertebrate DSCAM lacks the fly's splicing diversity. In mouse retina it is shared by cell type and seems to limit excess adhesion; match-triggered retreat is unestablished.
cards.quote: Vertebrate DSCAM and DSCAML1 are not spliced this way and cannot supply this diversity.
cards.section: Same problem, different molecules: the mouse

cards.front: Which protein family supplies individual surface identities in the tested mouse starburst amacrine-cell system?
cards.back: Clustered protocadherins; gamma protocadherins are required for these cells' dendritic self-avoidance.
cards.quote: mouse relies on the clustered protocadherins, adhesion proteins of the cadherin family,
cards.section: Same problem, different molecules: the mouse

cards.front: In mouse starburst cells, gamma protocadherin deletion disrupts sister-branch separation. Every starburst cell is then given the same single gamma protocadherin isoform. What happens to sister-branch separation and overlap between neighbours?
cards.back: Each cell's sister branches separate again, but neighbours also begin to avoid each other, reducing overlap. Matching isoforms make neighbours look like self.
cards.quote: Each cell's branches separated, but neighbouring cells also began to avoid each other.
cards.section: Same problem, different molecules: the mouse

cards.front: How could a small clustered protocadherin repertoire distinguish many neurons despite frequent sharing of individual isoforms?
cards.back: The leading model compares whole combinations. In one proposed zipper-like assembly, a mismatched isoform can stop chain growth, allowing cells with partly shared repertoires to remain distinguishable.
cards.quote: Comparing whole combinations, rather than single isoforms, would help, and it is a leading model:
cards.section: Same problem, different molecules: the mouse

cards.front: To which broad receptor class do odorant receptors belong?
cards.back: G protein-coupled receptors.
cards.quote: They are G protein-coupled receptors, and in rodents the family runs to about a thousand genes.
cards.section: A receptor that is also an address: smell

cards.front: With rare exceptions, an olfactory sensory neuron expresses {{c1::one}} odorant receptor gene.
cards.quote: Each olfactory sensory neuron in the nose expresses one odorant receptor gene, with rare exceptions.
cards.section: A receptor that is also an address: smell

cards.front: How does the organising principle of the olfactory map differ from that of a retina-to-tectum map?
cards.back: The olfactory map primarily groups sensory qualities by receptor identity, with coarse spatial order. The retina-to-tectum map preserves spatial relationships.
cards.quote: The olfactory map sorts what things are: it is mainly a map of qualities, with only coarse spatial order.
cards.section: A receptor that is also an address: smell

cards.front: The ball of neuropil where many olfactory sensory axons meet bulb-neuron dendrites is a {{c1::glomerulus}}.
cards.why: Neuropil is a tangle of axons, dendrites and synapses without cell bodies.
cards.quote: A glomerulus is a ball of neuropil, a tangle of axons, dendrites and synapses with no cell bodies,
cards.section: A receptor that is also an address: smell

cards.front: In mouse P2-expressing sensory neurons, retain the P2 promoter and an axon marker but remove the P2 receptor coding sequence. What happens to labelled axon convergence, and why?
cards.back: The labelled axons fail to form a P2 glomerulus and wander rather than converging. Promoter identity and location alone are insufficient; the receptor contributes to targeting.
cards.quote: the labelled axons failed to form a P2 glomerulus and wandered instead of converging.
cards.section: A receptor that is also an address: smell

cards.front: Mouse axons expressing M12 instead of P2 converge near the P2 glomerulus, far from M12's normal site. What does this imply about whether the receptor is a complete target address?
cards.back: It is only part of the address. Changing the receptor changes the target, but failure to reach the donor receptor's normal site shows that other neuronal features also matter.
cards.quote: So the receptor moved the axons, but not to a fixed donor address: it is part of the label, and other features of the neuron also count.
cards.section: A receptor that is also an address: smell

cards.front: A mouse neuron remains labelled from the P2 promoter after P2 receptor deletion but switches on another receptor gene. Why is it misleading to interpret its axon as lacking all receptor influence?
cards.back: The new receptor can confound the intended receptor-loss condition. A retained P2-promoter marker identifies the original population, not the absence of all receptor expression.
cards.quote: One complication: neurons left without a working receptor often switch on a second receptor gene, which makes the deletion harder to read than the swap.
cards.section: A receptor that is also an address: smell

cards.front: Why does convergence of axons expressing the same odorant receptor not establish direct homophilic adhesion between those receptors?
cards.back: Matching odorant receptors are not known to bind each other on axons. They are thought to influence other surface molecules that sort the axons.
cards.quote: unlike Sidekick, it is not known to bind matching receptors on other axons.
cards.section: A receptor that is also an address: smell

cards.front: Removing surface protein Z causes branches from different neurons of one type to bundle and their cell bodies to clump. What additional observations would distinguish a spacing role from layer selection or self-avoidance?
cards.back: Score arbor sublamina, crossings among one cell's own branches, and overlap between neighbours separately. Rule: these are distinct outcomes. Wrong layers suggest targeting; excess sister-branch crossings suggest self-avoidance; same-type bundling with cell-body clumping suggests shared spacing. Bundling alone does not establish active retreat.
cards.quote: score three things separately: where the arbor ends in the layer, how often the cell's own branches cross or bundle,
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Protein Z binds identical copies in a binding test. Can this identify whether Z causes neuronal adhesion or repulsion? What follow-up observation would resolve the response?
cards.back: No. Observe what contacting, Z-matched neuronal branches do: remain together or retreat. Rule: binding identifies recognition, while cellular behaviour determines the response; the same homophilic chemistry can support opposite outcomes.
cards.quote: This shows how strictly each form binds its own kind, not what the cell does after binding.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A new neuronal surface protein has a clear expression pattern, but removing it gives normal-looking arbors. What checks are needed before concluding it has no targeting role?
cards.back: Verify removal at the relevant stage and whether the measurements could detect the predicted phenotype; then consider redundant cues or compensation. Rule: expression alone establishes neither function nor response, and a normal-looking loss result does not exclude a role.
cards.quote: A normal-looking result does not rule out a role. Confirm that Z was removed at the right stage,
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: An axon reaches its target region and begins branching after a growth-cone pause. Does that establish correct synaptic partner selection, and why?
cards.back: No. Reaching the region and branching are earlier targeting stages; finding the correct place and choosing a partner still remain.
cards.quote: Targeting can be broken into four stages: reach the target region, slow down and branch, find the right place, and choose the right partner.
cards.section: Stages of targeting

cards.front: In a random-choice fly Dscam1 model, two neurons each use 20 of 19,008 ectodomains. Using expected overlap = 20 × 20 ÷ menu size, calculate their expected shared isoforms and the fraction of one cell's set shared.
cards.back: Expected overlap = 20 × 20 ÷ 19,008 ≈ 0.021 isoforms, about 0.02. Shared fraction = 0.02104377 ÷ 20 ≈ 0.00105, about 0.1%. These are model averages, not a retreat threshold.
cards.quote: Take the full fly menu of 19,008 ectodomains and suppose each neuron uses 20 of them at random.
cards.section: Why some isoform sharing may be tolerated

cards.front: In the random-choice fly Dscam1 model, approximate the probability of sharing at least one isoform with any one neighbour as 2%. Assuming 20 independent neighbour encounters, what is the probability of at least one sharing neighbour, and does that determine retreat?
cards.back: P(at least one) = 1 − (1 − 0.02)^20 ≈ 0.332, about a third. Rule: many encounters amplify a small per-neighbour chance. This motivates tolerance of partial sharing but does not measure the biological trigger for retreat.
cards.quote: These calculations motivate the idea that recognition tolerates some sharing; they do not measure the biological trigger.
cards.section: Why some isoform sharing may be tolerated

cards.front: A random protocadherin model gives 90%–99.8% sharing of at least one isoform between neurons but only about 1 in 20 billion to 1 in 6 trillion identical sets. How does this bear on recognition by one shared isoform versus by combinations?
cards.back: A one-shared-isoform rule would often confuse neighbours with self, whereas combinations can remain distinctive. Rule: sister branches match across their sets while neighbours need only differ enough. The arithmetic supports combination-based recognition but does not prove an exact-match biological trigger.
cards.quote: The arithmetic shows why comparing whole combinations helps; it does not prove that an exact match is the only rule that could work.
cards.section: How 58 protocadherin genes can be enough

cards.front: An odorant-receptor swap changes axon targeting. Does that establish the proposed mechanism in which odour-independent receptor activity drives cAMP and changes guidance-receptor levels?
cards.back: No. Rule: changing a signal and shifting the endpoint supports a causal contribution, not a particular downstream mechanism. The cAMP model rests on a few receptor lines, and an independent test of its neuropilin-1 step did not support it.
cards.quote: That model rests on a few receptor lines, and an independent test of its neuropilin-1 step did not support it.
cards.section: A disputed model of receptor-driven targeting
